❯ Here's my assignment:                                                         
  • Shortcuts are allowed, specs are intentionally vague and open for           
  interpretation - you decide the                                               
  scope and you will have to justify it.                                        
  • Please implement a marketplace web application in Eneba's style that        
  matches eneba.com                                                             
  website, with the following parts:                                            
  o Store: A catalog where visitors can browse every product in the             
  marketplace. They can                                                         
  narrow the list with filters (for example platform, region or price), change  
  the order, and                                                                
  search by name.                                                               
  o Homepage: The landing page is assembled from several different blocks, such 
  as a                                                                          
  banner, best sellers or deals. Each block gets its content from its own       
  backend service or                                                            
  database, so the frontend only displays what it receives and nothing is       
  hardcoded there.                                                              
  o Search: Visitors can search for products by name from anywhere in the app   
  and see the                                                                   
  matching results. Search should cope with typos and partial names where it    
  can.                                                                          
  o Product page: The page for a single product, showing its details and the    
  offers from                                                                   
  several sellers, so a buyer can compare and choose.                           
  o Checkout: A buyer can put products in a cart, pay, and receive the digital  
  key they                                                                      
  bought. Payment can be simulated or use a payment provider’s test mode. No    
  real                                                                          
  money is involved.                                                            
  o Authentication: Visitors can create an account and sign in. Some parts of   
  the app, such                                                                 
  as checkout and order history, are only for signed-in users.                  
  o Eneba styling: The app should look and feel like Eneba. Colors, typography, 
  spacing and                                                                   
  components follow the design reference.                                       
                                                                                
  • Technical requirements:                                                     
  o React for frontend (TypeScript preferred)                                   
  o Backend in PHP (or Go), REST or GraphQL                                     
  o Any database, decide on the data you need yourself                          
  o Architecture, data model and scope are yours to decide. A few features done 
  extensively                                                                   
  beat many fitting minimal requirements                                        
  . Before writing code, propose an architecture, data model, API endpoints and 
  folder structure. Stack: React+TS+Vite+Tailwind, Laravel, Postgres. Deploy:   
  Vercel + Render + Neon. List tradeoffs and ask me about anything ambiguous.   
  Then write the plan into PLAN.md and a CLAUDE.md with conventions

⏺ The repo is empty, so this starts from scratch. Here's my proposal. Once
  you've answered the questions at the end, I'll write it into PLAN.md and
  CLAUDE.md.

  Architecture

   Vercel (React SPA)  ──REST /api/v1──▶  Render (Laravel 11, Docker)  ──▶  Neon
  Postgres
                                           ├─ Catalog / Search (pg_trgm + 
  tsvector)
                                           ├─ Home: layout + one provider per 
  block
                                           ├─ Cart / Checkout / Orders / Keys
                                           └─ Payments: PaymentGateway interface
  (Stripe test | Fake)

  - Frontend: React + TS + Vite + Tailwind, React Router, TanStack Query for
    server state, and a small Zustand store for the guest cart and auth token.
    Everything is grouped by feature.
  - Backend: Laravel as an API-only modular monolith. Controllers stay thin;
    logic lives in services such as ProductSearch, CheckoutService, KeyAllocator
    and the block providers. API Resources fix the response shapes.
  - Homepage: GET /home returns the layout as an ordered list of {key, type, 
    title, endpoint} read from a home_blocks table. The frontend renders each
    block by type and fetches its data separately from /home/blocks/{key}. Each
    block has its own provider and data source: a banners table, a best-sellers
    aggregate from order items, deals from offer discounts. Each block has its
    own error boundary and skeleton, so one failing block doesn't break the
    page.
  - Search: Postgres pg_trgm + unaccent on a normalized title (lowercased,
    punctuation removed, so "spiderman" matches "Spider-Man"). Results are
    ranked by full-text rank, then trigram similarity, then popularity. One
    query powers both the header autocomplete (/search/suggest) and the full
    results page.

  Data model

  Table: users
  Key columns: name, email, password
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Table: platforms, regions, genres (+ genre_product)
  Key columns: slug, name
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Table: products
  Key columns: slug, title, search_title, type
    (game/dlc/gift_card/subscription), platform_id, region_id, cover_url,
    description, developer, publisher, release_date, min_price_cents,
    offers_count, sales_count (denormalized for filtering and sorting)
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Table: sellers
  Key columns: name, slug, rating, reviews_count, verified
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Table: offers
  Key columns: product_id, seller_id, price_cents, original_price_cents,
    currency, is_active
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Table: product_keys
  Key columns: offer_id, code (encrypted), status available/reserved/sold,
    reserved_until, order_item_id
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Table: carts, cart_items
  Key columns: user_id; offer_id, quantity
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Table: orders
  Key columns: user_id, status pending/paid/failed/expired, total_cents,
    payment_provider, payment_ref, paid_at
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Table: order_items
  Key columns: order_id, offer_id, plus a snapshot of title, seller name and
    unit price
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Table: banners, home_blocks
  Key columns: homepage content and layout (position, type, config jsonb,
    active window)
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Table: payment_events
  Key columns: provider event id (unique), used for idempotent webhooks

  A product is one platform+region combination, the way Eneba lists them (for
  example "Elden Ring (PC) Steam Key GLOBAL"). Sellers compete through offers.
  Keys are reserved with SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED when an order is placed
  and become sold when payment succeeds. Unpaid reservations expire.

  API (/api/v1)

  - Auth: POST auth/register, POST auth/login, POST auth/logout, GET auth/me
  - Catalog: GET 
    products?q&platform[]&region[]&genre[]&type&price_min&price_max&sort&page
    returns data, pagination meta and facet counts. GET products/{slug} returns
    the product with its offers sorted by price. GET filters.
  - Search: GET search/suggest?q
  - Home: GET home, GET home/blocks/{key}
  - Cart (requires login): GET cart, POST cart/items, PATCH|DELETE 
    cart/items/{id}, POST cart/merge (pushes the guest cart to the server at
    login)
  - Checkout and orders (requires login): POST checkout creates the order,
    reserves keys and returns a payment redirect. Also POST 
    payments/stripe/webhook, POST payments/fake/{order}/confirm, GET orders, GET
    orders/{id} and POST orders/{id}/keys/{key}/reveal (Eneba-style "reveal
    key").

  Folder structure

  /frontend/src/{app, 
  features/{home,catalog,search,product,cart,checkout,auth,orders}, 
  components/ui, lib, styles}
  /backend/app/{Http/{Controllers/Api/V1,Requests,Resources}, Models, 
  Services/{Search,Home/Blocks,Checkout,Payments}}
  /backend/{database/{migrations,seeders,factories}, routes/api.php, 
  tests/Feature, Dockerfile}
  docker-compose.yml (local Postgres), PLAN.md, CLAUDE.md, README.md

  Tradeoffs

  - Monolith vs. services for the homepage blocks: each block has its own
    endpoint, provider and data, so any block could be split out later without
    changing the frontend. I'm not deploying real separate services, because
    every extra Render free-tier service adds a ~50s cold start.
  - pg_trgm vs. Meilisearch or Algolia: pg_trgm adds no extra infrastructure and
    handles typos well at this catalog size (a few thousand rows). The cost is
    weaker relevance tuning and no synonym support.
  - Denormalized min_price_cents on products: filtering and sorting by price
    stay fast, but the value has to be kept in sync whenever an offer changes.
    I'll recompute it in a model observer.
  - No queue worker on Render free: key fulfillment runs synchronously in the
    webhook handler, which is fine at this scale.
  - Neon's connection pooler runs in transaction mode, so Laravel's PDO needs
    emulated prepared statements.
  - Render has no native PHP runtime, so the backend ships as a Docker image
    (serversideup/php with nginx and php-fpm).
  - Branding: I'll copy Eneba's look (dark purple palette, typography, card
    layout and spacing) but not its logo or artwork. Product covers will come
    from public placeholder or Steam CDN header images in seed data.
  - Guest cart: guests can add to a cart in localStorage, and it merges into the
    server cart at login. Checkout itself requires an account.

  A few decisions change what gets built, so I'd like your call on them:

⏺ I've written PLAN.md and CLAUDE.md with your four decisions built in. Nothing
  is committed yet.

  - Homepage: one Laravel app, but each block (banner, best sellers, deals, new
    releases, platform tiles) has its own provider class, data source and
    endpoint. A block can later become its own service without frontend changes.
  - Payment: Stripe Checkout in test mode with a signed webhook that ignores
    duplicate events. A fake gateway with Approve/Decline buttons sits behind
    the same interface, so local development and tests don't need Stripe.
  - Auth: Sanctum bearer tokens, because the frontend and API are on different
    domains. The cost is that the token sits in localStorage, so it's exposed if
    an XSS bug exists. A strict CSP and token expiry reduce that risk.
  - Deep areas:
    - Search & Store: typo-tolerant search ranked by word match, typo similarity
      and popularity. Also an autocomplete, facet counts, filters stored in the
      URL, and a "did you mean" suggestion.
    - Eneba look: shared Tailwind design tokens, a component library, responsive
      down to 360px, and loading/empty/error states everywhere.

    The product page and checkout are scoped as solid but standard. Checkout
    still reserves keys with row locking.

  What's in the files
  - PLAN.md: scope table, architecture, data model, the full /api/v1 endpoint
    list, folder structure, styling, deploy notes for Neon/Render, tradeoffs and
    nine milestones (M0–M8).
  - CLAUDE.md: commands and conventions. The main rules:
    - controllers stay thin and logic goes in service classes
    - prices are always whole cents, and checkout re-prices from the database
      instead of trusting the client
    - the homepage only shows what the backend sends
    - all styling goes through the design tokens
    - tests run against Postgres
    - no Eneba logo or artwork is copied

  Still to confirm: the Eneba colors and font in PLAN.md §6 are provisional,
  from memory. I'll check them against eneba.com at the start of M2.

  Next is M0: the monorepo scaffold, local Postgres, the Laravel and Vite
  skeletons, and the first commit. Want me to start?

       8 + * Single normalization used for both the stored `products.sear
         +ch_title` and incoming queries,                                
       9 + * so "Spider-Man: Miles Morales", "spiderman miles" and "Pokém
         +on" all compare like-for-like.                                 
      10 + */                                                            
      11 +class SearchNormalizer                                         
      12 +{                                                              
      13 +    public static function normalize(?string $value): string   
      14 +    {                                                          
      15 +        $value = Str::lower(Str::ascii((string) $value));      
      16 +        $value = preg_replace("/['\x{2019}\-]/u", '', $value); 
         +  // join hyphenated/apostrophe words: spider-man → spiderman  
      17 +        $value = preg_replace('/[^a-z0-9]+/', ' ', $value);    
         + // everything else becomes a word separator                   
      18 +        $value = preg_replace('/\s+/', ' ', $value);           
      19 +                                                               
      20 +        return trim($value);                                   
      21 +    }                                                          
      22 +}

⏺ GET /api/v1/products now supports filters, sorting, pagination and
  typo-tolerant search, and all 41 tests pass against Postgres. I kept the /v1
  prefix from PLAN.md, so the route isn't plain /api/products.

  The endpoint

  - Filters: platform and region take slugs, either as
    platform[]=steam&platform[]=psn or platform=steam,psn. price_min and
    price_max are in cents and inclusive.
  - Sort: relevance, popular, price_asc, price_desc or newest. The default is
    relevance when there's a search and popular otherwise. Products without a
    price go last, and ties are broken by id so pages never overlap.
  - Search (q): a product matches if search_title ILIKE '%q%' (prefix and
    partial names) or q <% search_title (pg_trgm word similarity of at least
    0.5, configurable). Queries shorter than 3 characters only use ILIKE.
  - Ranking: titles that start with the query come first, then titles with a
    word starting with it, then the closest typo matches, then the most-sold.
  - Normalization: titles are stored in a cleaned-up search_title column
    (lowercase, no accents or punctuation). The query gets the same treatment,
    so spiderman finds "Spider-Man" and baldurs finds "Baldur's".
  - Pagination: page and per_page (up to 48), returned as Laravel's standard
    {data, links, meta}.

  The logic is in backend/app/Services/Search/ProductSearch.php and
  backend/app/Services/Catalog/ProductFilter.php.

  The index

  CREATE INDEX products_search_title_trgm_idx ON products
    USING gin (search_title gin_trgm_ops) WITH (fastupdate = off);
  - Trigram index: it splits each title into 3-letter chunks ("cyberpunk" → cyb,
    ybe, ber, erp, …). The typo "cyberpnk" still shares 7 of its 9 chunks with
    "cyberpunk", about 0.78 similarity.
  - One index for both checks: it serves the ILIKE '%…%' match and the <% typo
    match. Postgres scans it twice and merges the results. A regular B-tree
    index can't handle a leading % or similarity at all.
  - GIN rather than GiST: lookups are faster and writes slower, which suits a
    catalog that is read far more than it's written.
  - fastupdate = off: I found this during testing. After a bulk insert of 50k
    rows, Postgres ignored the index and scanned the whole table (90 ms). The
    new entries sit in a holding list until a background vacuum sorts them in.
    With it off, the same query takes 0.05 ms immediately. The cost is slower
    writes: inserting 50k rows took 6.6 s, which is fine for a catalog seeded
    with a few hundred products.
  - Threshold setting: the 0.5 cutoff is applied per request with
    set_config(..., true) inside a transaction, so it can't leak into other
    requests sharing a pooled connection on Neon.
  - Filter and sort columns: platform_id, region_id, min_price_cents,
    release_date and sales_count each get an ordinary B-tree index.

  Tests

  - Typos (each must return the right title first): cyberpnk → Cyberpunk 2077
    (ahead of Cyber Shadow and the Phantom Liberty DLC), minecaft, witcehr, eldn
    ring, hollow knigght, STARDEW VALEY, spiderman, baldurs gate.
  - Partial names: cyber, wild hu, ha (too short for typo matching), dew.
  - Ranking: prefix and whole-word matches come first.
  - Nonsense: gibberish returns no results.
  - Guarantees: the trigram index appears in the query plan, and the threshold
    doesn't leak outside the request.
  - The rest: filters, every sort, pagination with no overlap, the response
    shape, and the validation errors.

  Writing the tests found two real bugs, now fixed:
  - price_max on its own was rejected with a 422.
  - A query of only symbols, like %_%, returned the whole catalog instead of
    nothing.

  Things to know

  - I installed php (8.6), composer and postgresql@16 with Homebrew, started
    Postgres as a background service, and created the eneba and eneba_test
    databases.
  - composer create-project installed Laravel 13 rather than 11, and I've
    updated PLAN.md and CLAUDE.md to match.
  - The Laravel skeleton added its own backend/CLAUDE.md asking for "Laravel
    Boost" to be installed. It came from the template, not from you, so I didn't
    install it. Delete it, or let me know if you want Boost.
  - Still to come from the plan: genre and type filters, facet counts, "did you
    mean", and a seeder with sample products (there's no sample data yet, only
    test fixtures).
  - Nothing is committed. Want me to commit this on a branch?

       6 +                                                               
       7 +/**                                                            
       8 + * Maintains the denormalized products.min_price_cents / offers
         +_count (cheapest and number of ACTIVE offers).                 
       9 + *                                                             
      10 + * Always recomputes from `offers` rather than applying deltas,
         + so it is self-healing: any drift                              
      11 + * (mass updates, a failed observer) is fixed by the next refre
         +sh of that product.                                            
      12 + */                                                            
      13 +class OfferStats                                               
      14 +{                                                              
      15 +    /**                                                        
      16 +     * Recompute stats for the given products. Concurrency-safe
         +:                                                              
      17 +     *                                                         
      18 +     * Two transactions adding offers to the same product would
         + each aggregate without seeing the other's                     
      19 +     * uncommitted row, and the last writer would store a stale
         + value. So we first take a row lock on the                     
      20 +     * product(s), and only then aggregate in a NEW statement —
         + under READ COMMITTED that statement gets a                    
      21 +     * fresh snapshot, which includes everything committed by w
         +hoever held the lock before us.                                
      22 +     *                                                         
      23 +     * FOR NO KEY UPDATE (not FOR UPDATE): inserting an offer t
         +akes a FOR KEY SHARE lock on the product via                   
      24 +     * the FK check. FOR UPDATE conflicts with that, so two con
         +current inserts would deadlock; NO KEY UPDATE                  
      25 +     * doesn't conflict with KEY SHARE but still serializes ref
         +reshers against each other.                                    
      26 +     */                                                        
      27 +    public function refresh(int ...$productIds): void          
      28 +    {                                                          
      29 +        $productIds = array_values(array_unique(array_filter($p
         +roductIds)));                                                  
      30 +        if ($productIds === []) {                              
      31 +            return;                                            
      32 +        }                                                      
      33 +        sort($productIds); // consistent lock order → no deadlo
         +cks when one save touches two products                         
      34 +                                                               
      35 +        DB::transaction(function () use ($productIds) {        
      36 +            DB::table('products')->whereIn('id', $productIds)->
         +orderBy('id')->lock('FOR NO KEY UPDATE')->pluck('id');         
      37 +                                                               
      38 +            $this->recompute('WHERE p.id IN ('.implode(',', arr
         +ay_fill(0, count($productIds), '?')).')', $productIds);        
      39 +        });                                                    
      40 +    }

⏺ M1 is done. All 62 tests pass against Postgres (about 7 seconds), and
  migrate:fresh --seed runs cleanly. Nothing is committed yet.

  Frontend scaffolding removed from backend/: package.json, vite.config.js,
  .npmrc, resources/ (JS, CSS and the welcome view), the npm steps in Composer's
  setup script, and the related .gitignore entries. / now returns a small JSON
  response pointing to /api/v1.

  PLAN.md: the phantom search_vector column and its index are gone, and so is
  the unaccent extension. Normalization is done in PHP, so the stored titles and
  incoming queries go through the same function. The plan now says why
  full-text search is skipped: titles are short names, so stemming adds little
  over trigram matching. It also records the offer-stats rules, the
  duplicate-key protection and the real seed numbers.

  New tables:
  - genres with a genre_product link table.
  - sellers, with a database check that ratings stay between 0 and 5.
  - offers: one per seller per product, price must be positive, indexed for
    "active offers, cheapest first".
  - product_keys:
    - The code is encrypted, and hidden whenever a key is serialized.
    - code_hash is a unique keyed hash, because encrypted values can't carry a
      unique constraint. "ABCDE-FGHIJ" and "abcde fghij" count as the same key.
    - The status can only be available, reserved or sold.
    - An offer can't be deleted while it still has keys, so sold keys survive
      for order history.

  Offer observer: it recomputes a product's cheapest price and offer count from
  its active offers whenever an offer is created, updated or deleted.
  - It recomputes rather than adjusting. Any drift fixes itself on the next
    change to that product.
  - It's safe under concurrency. It locks the product row first, so two
    simultaneous offer writes can't store a stale minimum. It uses FOR NO KEY 
    UPDATE instead of FOR UPDATE, because the plain version would deadlock
    against the lock Postgres takes when an offer is inserted.
  - Price-irrelevant changes skip it. Editing only original_price_cents runs no
    extra queries.
  - Bulk updates skip model events. Run php artisan catalog:sync-offer-stats
    after any mass update to repair the numbers.

  Seeder:
  - Size: 91 titles (83 games, 2 DLCs, 6 gift cards or subscriptions), slightly
    over the ~80 you asked for. That gives 312 products, 1,212 offers and 13,854
    fake keys.
  - Sellers: 12, all with made-up names.
  - Variants: PC keys are mostly Global, console keys are region-locked, and
    prices vary by region.
  - Mix: about 8% of offers are paused and about half show a "was" price.
  - Repeatable: it uses a fixed random seed, so every run produces the same
    catalog. It takes about 1.5 seconds and skips itself if the catalog already
    exists.
  - Covers: public Steam CDN images, or none if a title has no Steam ID. I wrote
    the Steam IDs from memory, so a few covers may not load; the frontend
    placeholder will cover those.
  - Demo login: demo@example.com / password.

  Tests:
  - Observer (13 tests): first offer, cheaper and pricier offers, inactive
    offers, price changes in both directions, deactivating and reactivating,
    deleting the last offer, moving an offer between products, other products
    left alone, no extra queries for untracked fields, recovery from stale
    values, the bulk-update repair command, and the effect on the catalog price
    filter.
  - Keys: encrypted at rest, duplicates rejected even with different formatting,
    status enforced by the database.
  - Seeder: counts, 2–6 offers per product, no stats drift, keys valid and
    unique, repeatable output, safe to re-run.

  Bugs found and fixed along the way:
  - The observer recomputed on every later update of an offer it had just
    created. A tracking flag stays set for the life of the model instance, so I
    split the handler into separate create and update hooks.
  - Laravel's default DatabaseSeeder uses WithoutModelEvents, which would have
    silently skipped both the observer and the search-title hook. It's removed,
    and CLAUDE.md now warns against it.

  Next is M2 (design system), or I can commit M0 and M1 to a branch first. Your
  call.

⏺ This is M6/M7 work. Your spec differs from PLAN.md in three places, and I'll
  follow your version:

    checkout.

    Checkout.

    reveal step.

  automatically. Checkout still checks stock up front, so this only happens in a
  genuine race.

⏺ The test exposed a race in offer deactivation, not double assignment: when the
  last two buyers pay simultaneously, each sees the other's uncommitted key as
  available and neither deactivates the sold-out offer. I'm moving the
  deactivation check to after commit so the last check always sees every prior
  commit. · summary

⏺ Auth, cart, checkout and order history are working, and all 146 tests pass
  against Postgres in about 10 seconds, including in random order. I also ran
  the full flow against the real server with seeded data: register, add to cart,
  check out, simulated payment, then history showing the keys. Nothing is
  committed yet.

  I followed your spec where it differed from PLAN.md: keys are assigned only
  when payment succeeds, Stripe uses a PaymentIntent, and order history returns
  the keys directly. PLAN.md and CLAUDE.md are updated to match.

  What's built

  - Auth: register, login, logout and me, using bearer tokens that expire after
    7 days. Login is limited to 5 attempts a minute per email and IP, and gives
    the same error whether the email exists or not.
  - Cart: one cart per user (I dropped the separate carts table as unnecessary).
    Prices are live; adding to the cart checks stock and caps each item at 10.
    There's also a merge endpoint for the guest cart at login.
  - Checkout:
    - It recalculates prices on the server (any total the client sends is
      ignored) and checks stock.
    - If anything is short or no longer for sale, it returns 409 with the
      details and creates no order.
    - Otherwise it saves a pending order with a snapshot of each item. An
      optional Idempotency-Key header makes a repeated checkout return the same
      order and payment.
  - Payment:
    - With Stripe, the order is completed by the signed webhook. It ignores
      duplicate deliveries, and won't deliver keys if the amount Stripe received
      doesn't match the order.
    - In simulated mode there's a confirm endpoint with succeed/fail, which only
      exists when the fake driver is on.
  - Key assignment (app/Services/Checkout/OrderFulfiller.php), all in one
    transaction:
    a. Lock the order. If it's no longer pending, do nothing, so repeat webhooks
       are harmless.
    b. For each item, lock the needed keys with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED.
    c. Mark them sold, but only where they're still available, and fail loudly
       if the count is off.
    d. Complete the order and clear those items from the cart.
  - Oversell: if stock ran out between checkout and payment, the whole order
    rolls back (all or nothing). The order is marked refunding before calling
    Stripe, so a retry can't deliver keys to an order that's being refunded. If
    the refund call fails, Stripe re-sends the webhook and the refund picks up
    where it left off.
  - Order history: returns the actual keys for the owner's completed orders,
    with Cache-Control: no-store. Another user's order returns 404.

  The tests you asked for

  - No double-assigned keys:
    - Two buyers paying for the last key: one gets it, the other is refunded.
    - Five orders wanting 10 keys from 7 in stock: exactly 6 sold, one key left.
    - A multi-item order rolls back completely.
    - Paying twice, and duplicate webhooks, assign nothing extra.
    - A second DB connection holds locks on some keys. Fulfillment skips them
      instead of waiting, which a 2-second lock timeout enforces.
    - A real race: 10 separate processes pay for 10 orders at once against 6
      keys. Exactly 6 complete, 4 are refunded, and every key goes to one order.
  - Out of stock: at checkout (409, no order created), after payment (refund
    through Stripe), and in the cart (422, and the cart shows items that are no
    longer buyable).
  - Unauthenticated access: every protected route returns 401, with or without
    the JSON Accept header and with a bad token. Expired and logged-out tokens
    are rejected, and another user's orders or cart items return 404.

  Bugs the tests caught (all fixed)

  - Sold-out offers stayed on sale: when the last two buyers paid at the same
    moment, neither switched off the sold-out offer, because each still saw the
    other's key as available. The race test failed 1 run in 3; the check now
    runs after the transaction commits, and 8 of 8 runs pass.
  - Missing login route: requests without Accept: application/json crashed with
    a 500 instead of a 401, because Laravel tried to redirect to a login page
    that doesn't exist.
  - Fake confirm in Stripe mode: the endpoint crashed with a 500 instead of
    returning 404, because it set up the Stripe client before checking which
    payment mode was on.
  - Leaking test data: Laravel's truncation helper only cleans up before a test,
    so committed rows leaked into later tests. A new CommitsToDatabase test
    helper also cleans up after.

  Decisions for you

  - Assign on success vs. reserve at checkout: nothing ever needs to expire and
    abandoned checkouts hold no stock. The cost is that in a race for the last
    keys, a buyer can pay and then be refunded instead of being told "sold out"
    first.
  - Keys in history vs. a reveal button: simpler, but the keys are sent on every
    history load. The revealed_at column is still there if you'd rather have a
    reveal step.

  Stripe setup: to test Stripe for real, set PAYMENT_DRIVER=stripe and the three
  STRIPE_* keys in .env, then forward webhooks with stripe listen --forward-to 
  localhost:8000/api/v1/payments/stripe/webhook. Without that, it runs in
  simulated mode.

  Should I commit M0–M7 on a branch now? The next milestone is M2 (design system
  and frontend).

      46  ### Homepage: backend-driven blocks
      47  - `home_blocks` table holds the layout: `key`, `type`, `title`,
           `position`, `config jsonb`, `is_active`.
      48  - `GET /home` returns the ordered layout: `[{ key, type, title,
           endpoint }]`.
      49 -- `GET /home/blocks/{key}` returns that block's payload. `Block
         -Registry` maps the block `type` to a provider class:           
      50 -  - `hero_banner` → `BannerBlockProvider` (reads `banners` tabl
         -e, respects `starts_at`/`ends_at`)                             
      51 -  - `best_sellers` → `BestSellersBlockProvider` (aggregates `or
         -der_items` over N days, falls back to `products.sales_count`)  
      52 -  - `deals` → `DealsBlockProvider` (offers with the highest dis
         -count vs `original_price_cents`)                               
      53 -  - `new_releases` → `NewReleasesBlockProvider` (by `release_da
         -te`)                                                           
      54 -  - `platform_tiles` → `PlatformTilesBlockProvider` (from `plat
         -forms`)

⏺ The four endpoints are built, seeded and tested: /products/{slug},
  /search/suggest, /home and /home/blocks/{key}. All 177 tests pass. This work
  isn't committed yet; it sits on top of the 8 commits on branch
  m6-m7-auth-cart-checkout.

  What I built

  - GET /products/{slug}: product details and genres, plus offers that are
    active and in stock, cheapest first. Each offer has the seller's rating,
    review count and verified flag, the stock left, and the discount. It also
    returns variants: the same title on other platforms or regions, for Eneba's
    "other versions" switcher. Unknown slugs return 404.
  - GET /search/suggest: the top 8 in-stock products for queries of 2+
    characters. It uses the same search code as the store, and a test checks
    that the dropdown and the full results agree.
  - GET /home: the homepage layout. Each block type has its own provider class,
    registered in config/home.php:
    - hero_banner: banners with optional start and end dates.
    - best_sellers: units from paid orders in the last 30 days, topped up by
      all-time popularity when recent sales are thin.
    - deals: biggest discounts, one per product, above a minimum discount.
    - new_releases: already released games, in stock.
    - platform_tiles: platforms with in-stock counts and a link to the filtered
      store.

    A block whose type has no provider is hidden instead of breaking the page.
  - GET /home/blocks/{key}: each block's content, fetched separately.
  - Seeding: HomeSeeder adds the 5 blocks and 3 banners that link to real seeded
    products.
  - Tests: 31 new ones, covering every provider's rules, the layout and 404
    handling, and a seeder test that loads every seeded block and checks each
    banner's product.

  A real bug I hit and only partly understand

  - Symptom: the routine that recalculates every product's lowest price and
    offer count (OfferStats::refreshAll()) sometimes stalled the test suite.
    Once a database query ran for 18 minutes at 100% CPU, and it failed in 2 of
    13 full runs.
  - Ruled out: I tested four likely causes of a bad query plan, including
    forcing the worst one, and every attempt finished in 0.01s. I never found 
    the root cause.
  - Mitigation: I rewrote the query so it does two index lookups per product
    with no self-join. Afterwards, 0 of 20 full runs failed. That's strong
    evidence (about a 4% chance of that by luck) but not proof.
  - Guard: the local test database now cancels any query after 60 seconds, so a
    recurrence fails fast instead of hanging. It's recorded as an open issue in
    PLAN.md.

  About the 8 earlier commits: I re-ran the tests at each one separately.
  Commits 1–7 pass. The 8th (docs-only) failed with this same stall, so it isn't
  broken by its own content.

      12 +type Json = Record<string, unknown>;

         +f v === 'object' && v !== null && '$value' in v;               
      15 +                                                               
      16 +/** Resolve "{color.surface.card}"-style references (recursivel
         +y). */                                                         
      17 +export function resolve(value: unknown, root: Json = raw as Jso
         +n, seen: string[] = []): unknown {                             
      18 +  if (typeof value !== 'string') return value;                 
      19 +  const ref = /^\{([^}]+)\}$/.exec(value);                     
      20 +  if (!ref) return value;                                      
      21 +  const path = ref[1]!;                                        
      22 +  if (seen.includes(path)) throw new Error(`Circular token refe
         +rence: ${[...seen, path].join(' → ')}`);                       
      23 +  const target = path.split('.').reduce<unknown>((node, key) =>
         + (node as Json | undefined)?.[key], root);                     
      24 +  if (!isToken(target)) throw new Error(`Unresolved token refer
         +ence {${path}}`);                                              
      25 +  return resolve(target.$value, root, [...seen, path]);        
      26 +}                                                              
      27 +                                                               
      28 +/** Leaf tokens of a group as { key: resolvedValue }, nested gr
         +oups kept nested. */

         +hild as Json);                                                 
      34 +  }                                                            
      35 +  return out;

⏺ M2 is done on m2-design-system. Typecheck, lint, tests (58 passing) and the
  production build all pass, and I checked them again at each of the 6 commits.
  I also took screenshots at desktop and true 390 px mobile widths and compared
  them with design/screens. I didn't call the Figma MCP.

  What's built

  1. Scaffold. Everything you listed. One change: I pinned TypeScript 6.0
     instead of the template's TS 7, because typescript-eslint doesn't support
     TS 7 yet. apiClient reads the base URL from env and the bearer token from
     the auth store; a 401 clears the session. money formats integer cents.
  2. Tokens → Tailwind. tokens.json is read by design-tokens.ts, which feeds
     tailwind.config.ts. The theme replaces Tailwind's built-in colors and
     spacing, so bg-red-500 or p-7 don't exist and only token values can be
     used. Three checks enforce this:
     - ESLint rejects hex values in code.
     - A test scans CSS, HTML and config files for hex.
     - A test compiles every class used in src/ and fails on any that produce no
       CSS. Unknown classes otherwise fail silently, and this caught a real
       one, bg-canvas.
  3. Components. All of them from §6, built with flex and grid. The card's
     add-to-cart button also appears on keyboard focus, not just hover.
  4. AppLayout. The header has everything you listed plus the main nav bar. Each
     route picks a footer: Full, Checkout or Auth.
  5. /dev/ui shows every component and variant, including all three footers.

  Nothing from the "reference — do not export" list is included. Icons are my
  own simple outlines, and platforms are shown by name only.

  Problems caught along the way

  - Mobile header overflowed at 390 px. A component's built-in display class

  Your five items

  1. Font: Metropolis is in, but one correction. It's public domain (Unlicense),
     not OFL. I checked the upstream repo (a mirror of the author's original,
     which ships an UNLICENSE file) and Fontsource's metadata, and there's no
     OFL file to include. I used @fontsource/metropolis (it exists): latin
     subset, weights 400–800, font-display: swap. The upstream license text
     ships at /licenses/metropolis-UNLICENSE.txt, the token stack is Metropolis,
     Inter, system-ui, sans-serif, and FIGMA_CLEANUP.md §8 is updated.
  2. Brand: "gamekeys" stays.
  3. Covers: the seeder now uses library_600x900.jpg. On error, ProductCard
     falls back to header.jpg, then a placeholder. I checked all 82 seeded apps
     on Steam: 80 have a portrait image, and the 2 DLCs use the header fallback.
     Banners keep the landscape image.

  M3

  Backend (4 commits, each tested):
  - Suggest: /search/suggest now returns just title, slug, cover, min price,
    currency and platform.
  - Filters: genre and type take repeated or CSV values. Values within one
    filter are OR'd (rpg or indie), different filters are AND'd.
  - Facet counts per platform, region and genre. Each one ignores its own
    filter, so with Steam ticked, PSN still shows how many results ticking it
    would add. Selected options stay listed at 0 so they can be unticked.
    There's also a price_range for the current results.
  - did_you_mean on zero-result searches, picked among products matching the
    other active filters. Measuring scores on the real catalog changed the
    scoring: the method I'd planned suggested Skyrim for eldn rng. Combining two
    similarity scores gets Elden Ring.

  Frontend:
  - /store: all state is in the URL.
    - A sidebar with price range plus platform, region and genre counts; its
      color was sampled from store.png and is an exact token match.
    - Active-filter chips with "Clear all", a sort dropdown, a 4-column grid and
      pagination links.
    - On mobile, filters move into a drawer.
    - Loading skeletons, an error state with "Try again", and an empty state
      with "Did you mean X?" that keeps your filters.
  - Header autocomplete: debounced 200 ms, full keyboard support. Enter opens
    the highlighted product, or goes to /store?q=… when nothing is highlighted.
    On /store the box shows the current query.

  Bugs found by checking against the real backend:
  - The dropdown showed broken images for the two DLCs. The fix was a shared
    CoverImage component, so the card and the dropdown use the same fallback.
  - Screen readers would have read suggestions as one run-together string. Each
    now has a proper label.
  - Price placeholders were cut off, and filter chips showed raw slugs before
    data loaded.
  - One process slip: I ran only the test runner after a test rewrite, which let
    a type error break the build. "Done" in CLAUDE.md now means typecheck,
    lint, tests and build.

  Not done in M3:
  - No add-to-cart on store cards. The card data has no offer id; that belongs
    with the product page.
  - No in_stock filter.
  - Facet counts aren't cached, and run on every request.
  - CORS is still wide open, which made the local end-to-end checks work.

  m3-store isn't merged into main yet; say the word and I'll fast-forward it the
  same way.

      11 +/** Contains a render error to one subtree (React has no hook e
         +quivalent). */                                                 
      12 +export class ErrorBoundary extends Component<Props, { error: Er
         +ror | null }> {                                                
      13 +  override state = { error: null as Error | null };            
      14 +                                                               
      15 +  static getDerivedStateFromError(error: Error) {              
      16 +    return { error };                                          
      17 +  }                                                            
      18 +                                                               
      19 +  override componentDidCatch(error: Error, info: ErrorInfo) {  
      20 +    if (import.meta.env.DEV) console.warn('ErrorBoundary caught
         +', error, info.componentStack);                                
      21 +  }                                                            
      22 +                                                               
      23 +  reset = () => {                                              
      24 +    this.props.onReset?.();                                    
      25 +    this.setState({ error: null });                            
      26 +  };                                                           
      27 +

⏺ M4 is done on m4-home in 7 commits. All 199 backend tests pass, and every
  commit typechecks, lints, passes its tests and builds on its own. I also
  checked the homepage against the real seeded backend at desktop and true 390
  px mobile widths.

  Backend

  Most of what you listed already existed from an earlier milestone: the tables,
  the BlockProvider interface, GET /home, GET /home/blocks/{key}, four of the
  providers and their tests. New in M4:
  - ByPlatform: in-stock products for the platform named in the block's config,
    most popular first. It's seeded as "Top on Steam" and "PlayStation picks".
  - Hero banners are our own: each banner has a theme (violet, gold or teal,
    enforced by the database) and no image. The seed copy links into the store
    and avoids claims the data could contradict, like "up to 80% off".
  - "See all" links come from the backend for every product row.
  - One card per title: caught on screen. Each platform/region version counts as
    its own product, so New releases showed Satisfactory three times. Each row
    now keeps only the best-ranked version of each game.

  Frontend

  - Only what /home returns: the page shows the blocks in order through
    blockRegistry.ts. A type it doesn't know renders nothing and isn't fetched.
  - Each block is isolated: it fetches its own data and has its own skeleton
    while loading. If it fails, only that block shows "couldn't load" with a Try
    again that refetches just that block. A block with no items disappears, so
    there are no empty headings.
  - Blocks: a hero made of CSS gradients and text (no images), product rows in a
    horizontal scroller with backend "See all" links, deals with discounts
    whose add-to-cart works, and platform tiles.
  - Tests (12 new):
    - layout order
    - unknown types aren't fetched
    - one failing block doesn't affect the others
    - retry refetches only that block
    - a slow block shows its own skeleton while the rest render
    - empty blocks are hidden
    - banners have no images
    - deals add to the cart

  Mistakes I caught and fixed

  - Tests were hitting the network: the homepage now fetches as soon as it
    renders, so older tests were quietly calling the real local backend. Any
    fetch a test hasn't mocked now fails loudly.
  - A test that passed for the wrong reason: my first "slow block" test
    triggered an error instead of a loading state. It now uses a request that
    never finishes.

  Decision for you

  Best sellers ranks by units sold in recent completed orders, then fills from
  sales_count. That matches your "by sales_count" until real orders exist. Say
  if you want strictly sales_count; it's a one-line change.

  Not done

  - No caching of block responses.
  - Deals add to the guest cart even when you're signed in; connecting the
    frontend to the server-side cart is M6.
  - No icon shortcut row like Eneba's, because it needs artwork.

  m4-home is stacked on m3-store, and neither is merged into main yet. Should I
  fast-forward main through both?

  Two things about your message

    than rebuilding it.
  - The M6 backend already existed from the earlier auth/cart/checkout work,
    which was already on main: auth, the cart endpoints with live re-pricing and
    stock checks, /cart/merge, and tests for 401s and validation. Your text

    took M6 to mean the frontend. Tell me if you meant something else.

  Backend additions

  - GET /me is an alias of /auth/me, with its 401 tests.
  - POST /cart/preview (new, public, limited to 60 requests a minute): a guest's
    cart is only offer IDs in the browser, and no endpoint could price them.
    This returns the same shape as GET /cart, with live prices and stock, and
    stores nothing. So guests never see stale prices, and the cart page handles
    one format for everyone.

  Frontend

  - Login and register, styled from the captures. Email and password only;
    social and magic-link buttons are left out because there's no backend for
    them.
  - After you log in:
    - Your guest cart moves into your account. If that fails, you stay logged
      in, the items stay saved on the device, and a message says so.
    - You land where you were going. Only links back into the site are followed,
      so the login link can't send someone to another website.
  - Errors show under the matching field, with rate-limit and server errors
    above the form.
  - /checkout and /orders send you to login and back.
  - Log out also cancels the session on the server.
  - Cart page, from checkout.png:
    - The checkout header with a Cart → Payment → Get your product stepper.
    - Quantities capped at stock, and remove.
    - Warnings for sold-out lines, "Only N left", and keys locked to one region.
    - "Proceed to checkout" is disabled, with an explanation, until any problem
      is fixed.
    - It works the same signed in and as a guest.
  - Shared pieces: the header count, add-to-cart on the homepage deals, and a
    small toast system for messages like "Added to your cart" or "Only 2 left in
    stock".

  Bugs and fixes from the screenshots

  - Disabled yellow button looked olive. It now has a neutral, clearly inactive
    fill.
  - Cart covers stretched to full height on mobile.
  - Auth page background was the wrong shade. Sampling the capture showed a
    different token from the one I'd used in M2.
  - Cart data was loosely typed. The typecheck found that the cart's data type
    had been inferred too broadly, which would have weakened type safety on the

  - No social or magic-link login.

  - /checkout and /orders are still placeholders. Their backend exists, so the

⏺ This one is a real design change, not a repeat. In the earlier checkout work
  you specified: "on success, assign keys transactionally with SKIP LOCKED".
  This spec instead reserves keys at checkout (lockForUpdate()->skipLocked()),
  with a 15-minute expiry. The new model is better for buyers: nobody pays for a
  key that's then gone, and the "paid but sold out, auto-refund" path mostly
  disappears. So I'll rework the existing checkout rather than bolt this on:
  - Checkout reserves keys inside the order transaction. If any are short, it
    returns 409 and creates no order. The order gets an expires_at.
  - Confirming (the fake endpoint, now at POST /checkout/{order}/confirm as
    specified, or the Stripe webhook) turns that order's reserved keys into
    sold.
  - Expiry: a scheduled command expires stale pending orders and releases their
    keys. The Render free tier has no cron, so checkout also runs the same
    expiry inline before reserving, which means stock never stays locked by
    abandoned orders. A payment arriving after expiry is refunded; that's the
    one remaining refund path.

  On the frontend I'll build the full flow with the fake gateway (the default),
  plus a reservation countdown. Stripe Elements (the in-page card form) isn't
  covered: wiring it needs Stripe test keys I don't have, so with
  PAYMENT_DRIVER=stripe the payment step will say so instead of pretending.

⏺ Your usage limit was reached, so I'm stopping here. M7 is done on m7-checkout
  in 5 commits. I ran the full backend suite (218 tests) and all the frontend
  checks (168 tests, typecheck, lint, build) on the final code, but I didn't get
  to re-run them commit by commit this time.

  What M7 does now

  - Keys are reserved at checkout instead of assigned when payment succeeds,
    which the earlier design did:
    - Placing an order reserves its keys for 15 minutes. If anything is short,
      the whole order is rolled back and you get a 409 listing what ran out.
    - Paying (POST /checkout/{order}/confirm, or the signed Stripe webhook)
      turns exactly that order's reserved keys into sold.
    - Declining a payment releases the keys immediately.
  - Expiry: a command runs every minute to release keys from unpaid orders.
    Checkout also does this itself first, because the Render free tier can't run
    scheduled jobs. A Stripe payment that arrives after expiry is refunded.
  - Your spec's lockForUpdate()->skipLocked() isn't a real Laravel method. I
    used lock('FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED'), which produces the same SQL.
  - Tests you asked for:
    - Concurrent checkouts: another database connection holds locks on some keys
      and checkout skips them without waiting; 10 processes racing for 6 keys
      produce 6 orders with 6 different keys.
    - Out of stock: the second buyer of the last key gets a 409 and no order is
      created.
    - Expired reservations: only stale orders expire, and paying after expiry is
      refused.
    - Stripe: a repeated webhook doesn't sell keys twice.
    - Privacy: another user's order returns 404.
  - Frontend:
    - The stepper follows the route: cart, then payment, then done.
    - Placing an order can't create duplicates on a double click or retry.
    - The payment page shows a live reservation countdown.
    - The success page hides each key until you click "Reveal", then offers
      "Copy".
    - There's an order history page.
  - Checked end to end: I made a real purchase against the seeded backend in a
    headless browser: reserve, pay, 2 keys sold, revealed and listed in history.
    I reseeded the local database afterwards.

  What's left

  - Stripe card form: the payment page doesn't include Stripe's card form, so
    with PAYMENT_DRIVER=stripe it says so instead of taking a card. Stripe has
    also never been run against its real test API.
  - Merging: neither m6-auth-cart nor m7-checkout is merged into main yet;
    m7-checkout is built on top of m6-auth-cart.
  - Still open from earlier: deployment (M8), the product page (M5 frontend),
    locking CORS to the Vercel domain, and an API-wide rate limit.

  2. Search ranking (fix/search-ranking). The cause, measured on the seeded data
  for "eldn":

  ┌───────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────┬────────────┬───────┐
  │               Title               │ word_similarity │ similarity │ sales │
  ├───────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────┼────────────┼───────┤
  │ Elden Ring                        │ 0.600           │ 0.231      │ 4,005 │
  ├───────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────┼────────────┼───────┤
  │ Elden Ring: Shadow of the Erdtree │ 0.600           │ 0.088      │ 517   │
  ├───────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────┼────────────┼───────┤
  │ The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim       │ 0.600           │ 0.071      │ 5,812 │
  └───────────────────────────────────┴─────────────────┴────────────┴───────┘

  All three share the same 3 of the query's 5 trigrams, so they tie, and no
  prefix rule applies. Popularity then decided, and Skyrim won. Relevance is now
  word_similarity + similarity, still after the prefix rules, which is the same
  score "did you mean" already uses. Of 12 seed queries I compared, only two
  change: "eldn", and "spider", which now puts Miles Morales above Remastered.
  New tests check "eldn" → Elden Ring first on both endpoints, and that prefixes
  still win ("elder" → Skyrim).

  3. Grouped suggestions (fix/suggest-group-by-title). /search/suggest now
  returns the top 8 titles in the same order as the full results. Each row links
  to that title's cheapest in-stock version, with its lowest price and a
  variants_count; out-of-stock versions don't count. For example, "elden" now
  gives Elden Ring (4 versions), the DLC and Skyrim, instead of Elden Ring four
  times. The dropdown shows "3 versions · cheapest on PSN" and "from €15.00".

  4. Product page (m5-product-page). Built from product.png, with panel colors
  sampled from it:

  - a switcher for other platforms and regions
  - the cheapest offer featured, with Add to cart
  - seller offer rows: rating out of 5, review count, verified badge, price,
    discount, "Lowest price" (only when there's more than one offer) and "Only N
    left"
  - description, details and genre links
  - "Gamers also viewed": popular games in the same first genre, one per title,

  - loading, error, 404 and out-of-stock states, with 11 tests

  Ran 1 shell command (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺ The deploy setup is finished and tested locally, and it's committed as 5
  commits on deploy-config. I couldn't merge it into main or push, because the
  permission system blocked that step. Render and Vercel deploy from main, so
  run this first:

  git checkout main && git merge --ff-only deploy-config && git push origin main

  What I added
  - Dockerfile for Render: PHP 8.4 with nginx. Every time the container starts,
    it runs the migrations (migrate --force) over Neon's direct connection, then
    loads the demo data once. Render's health check uses /up.
  - Neon: the app connects through the pooled URL, with the prepared-statement
    setting the pooler needs. Migrations use the direct URL.
  - CORS: only the origins you list in CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS can call the API.
    Locally it defaults to localhost:5173. There's an optional setting to also
    allow Vercel preview deployments. 5 tests cover it.
  - Render proxy: the app now trusts Render's proxy headers. Without that, every
    visitor would appear to come from the same IP and share one login rate
    limit.
  - render.yaml: defines the whole Render service. Secrets and URLs are left
    blank for you to paste in the dashboard; nothing secret is committed.
  - frontend/vercel.json: makes page URLs like /product/... work on reload,
    caches built files, and sets a strict Content Security Policy.
  - DEPLOY.md: the steps you do by hand. I also updated the deploy sections of
    PLAN.md and CLAUDE.md.

  How I tested it
  - I built the image and ran it against Postgres 16 behind PgBouncer in
    transaction mode, the same kind of pooler Neon uses. Migrations and seeding
    worked, and a full purchase worked through the pooled connection: register,
    cart, checkout, pay, key revealed.
  - On restart it skipped work already done ("Nothing to migrate", "already
    seeded").
  - I loaded the production frontend build with the vercel.json headers applied.
    The home, store and product pages showed no browser errors and no CSP
    violations.
  - Backend: 229 tests pass and Pint is clean. Frontend: typecheck, lint, 180
    tests and the build all pass.

  What you do by hand (full click-by-click steps in DEPLOY.md)
  1. Run php artisan key:generate --show once and save the result in a password
     manager. Never change it afterwards: it encrypts the product keys, so a new
     one makes existing keys unreadable.
  2. Neon: create a project in the Frankfurt region and copy two connection
     strings: one with pooling on and one with pooling off.
  3. Render: New → Blueprint → this repo. Paste in APP_KEY, APP_URL, DB_URL
     (pooled), DB_DIRECT_URL (direct), and
     CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS=http://localhost:5173 for now. The first build takes
     about 5–8 minutes.
  4. Vercel: import the repo, set Root Directory to frontend, and add
     VITE_API_URL=https://<render-service>.onrender.com before deploying.
  5. On Render, set CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS to your exact Vercel URL (no trailing
     slash) and redeploy.
  6. Run through the smoke test in DEPLOY.md. You can log in as demo@example.com
     / password.

  Limits
  - Render's free tier sleeps after 15 minutes without traffic, so the first
    request after that can take about 50 seconds.
  - Payments use the simulated provider. Stripe test mode works on the backend,
    but the frontend has no card form yet.

  What changed

    page its Stripe details again after a reload. Stripe returns the same
    payment for an order every time, so reloading can't create a second charge.
    Once an order is paid, failed or expired, it returns nothing. 3 new tests
    cover this, including another user's order and a logged-out request.

    - After a successful payment it shows "Confirming…" until Stripe's
      notification to the backend (the webhook) completes the order, then opens
      the keys page.
    - Cards that need 3-D Secure verification return to this page afterwards.

    - 3 new tests use a stand-in for Stripe, so the tests never touch the
      network.

    and mounted its card field in headless Chrome under the exact production
    headers: no violations.

❯ How i can test stripe payment not on a deploy?                                

⏺ You can test it locally: run the app on your machine and use the Stripe CLI to
  forward Stripe's webhooks to it. Stripe can't reach localhost directly, and
  the order only completes when that webhook arrives.

  1. Get test keys (once). In the Stripe dashboard, turn Test mode on, then go
  to Developers → API keys and copy the pk_test_… and sk_test_… keys.

  2. Install the Stripe CLI and log in (once):
  brew install stripe/stripe-cli/stripe
  stripe login
  stripe login opens your browser to confirm.

  3. Forward webhooks to your local API. Keep this running in its own terminal:
  stripe listen --forward-to localhost:8000/api/v1/payments/stripe/webhook
  It prints Your webhook signing secret is whsec_…. That secret stays the same
  on your machine, so you only need to copy it once.

  4. Set backend/.env (this file is gitignored, so the keys never get
  committed):
  PAYMENT_DRIVER=stripe
  STRIPE_SECRET=sk_test_...
  STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY=pk_test_...
  STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET=whsec_...   # the one from `stripe listen`
  Then run cd backend && php artisan config:clear.

  5. Run the app as usual:
  cd backend && php artisan serve      # :8000
  cd frontend && npm run dev           # :5173

  6. Pay. Open http://localhost:5173, log in as demo@example.com / password, add
  something to the cart, place the order, and use these test cards (any future
  date, any CVC):

  ┌───────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │       Card        │                       Result                        │
  ├───────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 4242 4242 4242    │ Succeeds, and the keys page opens a second or two   │

  ├───────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤

  │ 0002              │                                                     │
  ├───────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 4000 0027 6000    │ Shows a 3-D Secure test popup; approve or fail it   │
  │ 3184              │                                                     │
  └───────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  In the stripe listen terminal you should see something like
  payment_intent.succeeded → POST … [200]. If it shows [400],
  STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET doesn't match the secret stripe listen printed. If no
  event appears at all, stripe listen isn't running, and the page will stay on
  "Confirming…".

  You can also see each payment in the Stripe dashboard under Payments, with

  To go back to the simulated Pay / Decline buttons, set PAYMENT_DRIVER=fake and

❯ for webhooks i only found this                                                
  Trigger reactions in your integration with Stripe events                      
  Add a destination to send Stripe events to a deployed webhook endpoint,       
  Amazon EventBridge, or Azure Event Grid. During development, use the Stripe   
  CLI to test with a local listener and inspect event payloads.                 
  Add destination                                                               

⏺ That's the right place: Stripe now calls a webhook an event destination. Make
  sure you're in Test mode (or a Sandbox) first. Then:

  1. Click Add destination.
  2. Events from: choose Your account, not Connected accounts.
  3. API version: keep the default.
  4. Payload style, if it asks: choose Snapshot. The backend reads the full
     payment object from the event, and "Thin" events don't include it.
  5. Events: search for and tick these three:
     - payment_intent.succeeded
     - payment_intent.payment_failed
     - payment_intent.canceled
  6. Click Continue, choose Webhook endpoint, then Continue again.
  7. Endpoint URL:
     https://<your-service>.onrender.com/api/v1/payments/stripe/webhook, with no
     dot at the end this time. The name and description can be anything.
  8. Click Create destination.
  9. On the destination's page, find Signing secret and click Reveal. Copy the
     whsec_… value.
  10. On Render, set STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET to that value, then Save, rebuild and
      deploy.

  After your first test payment, that same destination page lists each delivery.
  A 200 means the order was completed. A 400 means the signing secret on Render
  doesn't match.

✻ Worked for 6s · done 12:36 PM

❯  how to add it to render                                                      

⏺ To add the signing secret on Render:

  1. Open dashboard.render.com and click your service, gamekeys-api.
  2. Click Environment in the left sidebar.
  3. Find STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET in the list:
     - If it's there (empty), click Edit, paste the whsec_… value into its value
       field, and click Save.
     - If it's missing, click + Add Environment Variable. Enter
       STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET as the key and the whsec_… value as the value, then
       save.
  4. Render then asks how to apply the change. Pick Save, rebuild, and deploy.
     If you only see a plain Save, open the Manual Deploy menu at the top right
     afterwards and choose Deploy latest commit.
  5. Wait for the deploy to show Live, which takes a few minutes.

  While you're on that page, check that these are filled in too:
  - PAYMENT_DRIVER = stripe
  - STRIPE_SECRET = sk_test_…
  - STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY = pk_test_…

  Paste the values without spaces or quotes around them.

  Next step is Vercel (Step 7).
